title: Augmented Reality: Coming Soon?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore augmented reality (AR): how it differs from virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality, the basics of how AR devices sense and render digital layers (time-of-flight sensors, stereo cameras, gyroscopes, GPS, facial tracking at about thirty frames per second), marker-based versus markerless AR, and the history from Ivan Sutherland's headset and Myron Krueger's Videoplace through the 1990s and Sixth Sense's 2009 TED talk, to Pokemon Go, the NFL first-down line, and Google Glass. They cover applications in retail, healthcare, navigation, military training, accessibility for people with sensory impairments, and museums and tourism. Hurdles discussed include bandwidth and latency (with 5G as a possible fix), hardware such as contact lenses and power sources, privacy, hacking, and over-reliance on apps. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about a disagreement over apple bobbing at trunk or treating.

segments.title: Opening banter and predictions about AR
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about a friend who predicted that AR glasses would be everywhere within a few years, and they debate whether that will happen. They set up the topic.

segments.title: Definition of AR and Pokemon Go
segments.summary: They define augmented reality as a computer-generated layer added to real life, possibly involving sight, touch, sound, or smell. They discuss how it differs from VR and cite Pokemon Go's success in 2016.

segments.title: AR vs mixed reality
segments.summary: The hosts use a soup can example to show a simple AR overlay compared with mixed reality, where occlusion lets real objects such as a hand cover digital information.

segments.title: How AR works: sensing and rendering
segments.summary: They give a layman's overview of computer vision, time-of-flight infrared sensors, stereo cameras, gyroscopes, GPS, and facial tracking, and say the output updates about thirty times per second. They also mention Snapchat and FaceTime filters.

segments.title: Navigation habits and tech reliance
segments.summary: The hosts compare their navigation habits, with Josh walking by compass and Chuck using maps, and talk about how people use phones to find direction.

segments.title: Marker-based vs markerless AR
segments.summary: They explain that marker-based AR relies on preloaded targets such as QR codes or landmarks, while markerless AR recognizes things like rivers and walkways without preloaded markers. Pokemon Go is given as an example. A soup recipe tangent follows.

segments.title: History: Sutherland, Krueger, and Sixth Sense
segments.summary: They trace AR history from Ivan Sutherland's wire-frame headset and Myron Krueger's Videoplace in the 1970s to the 2009 Sixth Sense TED talk, which used a projector, camera, and colored finger caps for gesture input. They also recall the first-down line on TV.

segments.title: Early AR uses and smartphone era
segments.summary: They discuss other early AR uses, including the NHL hockey puck overlay, an Esquire cover, Starbucks Valentines, and the 1990s beta Dancing in Cyberspace. They say smartphones pushed AR forward and note consumer apps like star maps and parking finders.

segments.title: Applications: tourism, military, shopping, healthcare, accessibility
segments.summary: The hosts discuss AR uses in museums, Pompeii, Gatwick Airport, Wikitude, military synthetic training environments, retail furniture and glasses try-ons, healthcare practice surgeries, and help for people with vision or hearing impairments.

segments.title: Hardware, bandwidth, and pitfalls
segments.summary: They describe the Asus Zenfone AR and Google Tango, then challenges such as bandwidth, latency, 5G, the need for better hardware and power for contact lenses, the risk of a career arms race, safety, hacking, privacy, and the Google Glass failure.

segments.title: Closing remarks and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the AR discussion and suggest revisiting it in five years. Then they read listener mail from Alex in London about a disagreement over apple bobbing at trunk or treating.
